title: Start Here
subtitle: A getting-started guide to Randall Young’s Project Atlas
intro: Project Atlas is a public guide to experiments, classroom activities, instruments, and their source records. You do not need to understand the whole archive to use it. Pick one question, try one thing, and follow the evidence.

software_aside.title: Make it your own
software_aside.status: A friendly heads-up. Some Atlas software is ready to run, some is a prototype, and some projects are still designs. Find the GitHub repo and start with its README.
software_aside.advice: You don’t have to start with a blank editor. Find the project’s GitHub repository, tell an AI coding assistant which board and sensor you have, and describe what you want the device to do. It can help you understand the existing code, adapt it to your setup, or work through a compiler error.
software_aside.bench_check: Then change one thing and try it. If you’re timing a robot, watch it move and measure where it stops. If you’re reading a sensor, compare its reading with something you can check independently. AI helps you get to that first experiment sooner. What you observe tells you what to change next.
software_aside.print_advice: Give an AI coding assistant the GitHub link, your board and sensor, and a small goal. Ask for one code change, then check what it actually does on your hardware.

evidence: A measured run, a simulated example, and a working dashboard are different kinds of evidence. Read the captions and validation notes before you draw a conclusion. A good first experiment is one you can explain and repeat.
